#### Once the fishermen’s protector, today Mumbadevi reigns over India’s financial hub
BY CHOODIE SIVARAM, BENGALURU
**M**UMBAI: SYNONYMOUS WITH BOLLYWOOD, industrialists, Gateway of India, the Bombay Stock Exchange and the Reserve Bank of India. The 12th wealthiest city in the world, it accounts for 87% of the Maharashtra state economy. Though best known as India’s financial capital, Mumbai is also one of India’s major migrant magnets, the ultimate big-city dream for small-town Indians wanting to prosper. Mumbai is home to countless success stories from across the generations, with innumerable celebrities who came here penniless and hit the jackpot.
And yet, very few know of the Goddess Mumbadevi, from Whom the city derives its name, Who protects and watches over Her people. “Our presiding Deity of Mumbai ensures that anyone who comes to Her abode seeking success is not deprived of realizing their dreams. She not only fulfills dreams but is the protector of this city from calamity,” Hemant Jadhav, manager of the Mumbadevi temple, told me during my visit.
![Image 1](http://ds.hinduismtoday.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/f0036-01-1024x666.jpg)
The temple is in one of the most congested parts of Mumbai
Umesh Bajpai, a local businessman, put it this way: “No one who comes to Mumbai seeking a better life remains unsuccessful. Whether they stay on the footpath or in mansions, the Goddess gives them their bread and butter, She is a wish-fulfilling Goddess. I myself met with a terrible accident some years ago and had to go through some surgeries. My family prayed to Mumbadevi and I recovered completely. Now the doctors say I’m absolutely fit, and ever since I haven’t had to take any medications.”
Jadhav relates, “A lot of people, even those living here for generations, are not aware of this ancient Mumbadevi temple. I have met so many people who are in their sixties and seventies who are coming here for the first time despite being in Mumbai from birth.”

#### Once the fishermen’s protector, today Mumbadevi reigns over India’s financial hub
In fact, one of my friends, Mahabala Bhat, a native of Karnataka who has lived in Mumbai for decades, heard about the temple for the first time when I expressed my desire to visit it.

#### **The Temple’s Story**
Locals narrate a legend where the Goddess killed a demon named Mumbarak and to honor his death-bed wish She agreed to join his name with Hers; and hence the name _Mumbadevi_. Her temple was originally built 500 years ago by the Koli fisherman community, when what is now Mumbai was a collection of seven islands with just 10,000 residents. She was their presiding Deity. The present murti is made of sand and is believed to be over 400 years old.
Around 1737, when the Bombay Government began enlarging the fortifications of the old town, the original temple was demolished. That first location is unknown, but in the 1800s Mumbadevi temple was in Bori Bunder where the Chatrapathi Shivaji Terminus railway station stands today. In 1845 a large reclamation project consolidated the seven islands into a single landmass. Thereafter the population grew rapidly.
In 1853 the British built a railway station at Bori Bunder, which also served as the headquarters of the Great Indian Peninsula Railway. The temple continued to exist on the railway platform.
In 1888 the magnificent architectural structure Victoria Terminus (now Chatrapathi Shivaji) railway station was built to replace the Bori Bunder station. The Mumbadevi temple was shifted to nearby Phansi Talao in the Esplanade. Subsequently the Esplanade was acquired by the British for parades and the temple moved to Dhobi Talao. At last, in the late 1800s, it made one final move to its current location. It now stands two miles north of the “Gateway of India” in the midst of Zaveri Bazar, Asia’s biggest jewelry market, which receives the majority of the country’s gold and rough diamond imports. The temple is also surrounded by the lucrative cloth, steel and iron markets.
The construction and management of the new ornate temple was entrusted to Pandushet Sonar, a merchant of considerable influence with the then government in Bombay. He took care of the temple, and his family inherited its management. Through the decades, management of the temple changed hands several times. As Mumbai expanded and its population grew, shops and houses mushroomed in the modest lanes around the temple.

#### **The Temple’s Story**
In 1952 the Charity Commissioner took over the temple’s affairs, and by court order a management trust was registered. The nine-member trust board is presently comprised of solicitors, chartered accountants, doctors and an industrialist. About 15,000 people visit daily, with the number going to over 25,000 on festival days.
Despite the cramped location and huge crowds, the temple is well maintained, clean and organized. As soon as one enters, it is impossible not to connect with the Goddess. Mumbadevi sits majestically on Her lion, infusing power and confidence in Her devotees as they surrender to Her. Adjoining the sanctum sanctorum of Mumbadevi is the imposing shrine of Jagadamba with Annapooraneshwari (both forms of the Goddess), showering benevolence on worshipers. The ornate walls with exquisite paintings of Gods and Goddesses blend into the divinely charged ambiance.
![Image 2](http://ds.hinduismtoday.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/f0037-01.jpg)
Some of the 15,000 visitors a day
The temple is open from 6:30am to 10 pm. As in all Devi temples, the celebration of Navaratri is of primacy. At Mumbadevi, four navaratris are celebrated in a year. Besides the Chaitra Navaratri (March/April) and Sharad Ashwin Navaratri (September/October), the lesser known Gupta Navaratris during Maagh (January/February) and Ashaada (June/July) are also celebrated.
The temple is one of the richest in the city. Its income is used to administer the temple and conduct festivities. “We are handling public money. We engage in charity and run an old age home in Ahmedabad. We provide scholarships to deserving students and medical aid to the poor. We also help other institutions engaged in social service,” confirms Jadhav.

#### **The Temple’s Story**
A few years back the temple ran into a controversy with reports of a government takeover. An investigation into the temple’s finances and administration by the Charity Commission found nothing amiss, and the issue was dropped. Following the infamous bomb blasts in 1993, three of which were in the vicinity of the temple, Mumbai police have greatly increased security in the area.
One devotee, Sushma Baadakar, told me of two great miracles in her life she attributes to the Goddess. The first, a property dispute, was resolved shortly after a chance visit to the temple in 2012 with her brother. She said, “The visit brought me under the protection of the Goddess.” Later, faced with cancer, she recounts, “At every stage of my treatment I saw miracles that left the doctors baffled. I still feel Mumbadevi is always with me, guiding every moment of my life.”
Whether Mumbai residents are aware of Mumbadevi or not, whether they visit her shrine or not, it is strongly believed that She protects anyone who comes to Her land. From the Ambanis to Bollywood stars and singers, innumerable people who came to this city seeking greener pastures, many of them with humble beginnings staying on pavements and railway platforms, have become rich and famous. Mumbadevi has remained true to Her legend as the wish-fulfilling Goddess who protects Her people.

**Monaco-Ville** ([[mɔnakɔ vil]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French"); [Monégasque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mon%C3%A9gasque_dialect "Monégasque dialect"): _Mu̍negu-A̍utu_)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco-Ville#cite_note-1) is the southcentral [ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_divisions_of_Monaco "Administrative divisions of Monaco") in the [Principality of Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco-Ville#cite_note-2) Located on a [headland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headland "Headland") that extends into the [Mediterranean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco-Ville#cite_note-3) it is nicknamed [The Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_of_Monaco "Rock of Monaco") (French: _Le Rocher_; Monégasque: _A Roca_). It holds most of the country's political and judicial institutions: the [Prince's Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince's_Palace_of_Monaco "Prince's Palace of Monaco"), the [town hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipality_of_Monaco "Municipality of Monaco"), the government, the [National Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Council_(Monaco) "National Council (Monaco)") (parliament of Monaco), the [Municipal Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communal_Council_of_Monaco "Communal Council of Monaco"), the courts and a prison (hanging on The Rock).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco-Ville#cite_note-4)

Monaco-Ville is one of the four traditional [quarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarter_(urban_subdivision) "Quarter (urban subdivision)") ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _quartiers_) of Monaco; the others are [La Condamine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Condamine "La Condamine"), [Monte Carlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo "Monte Carlo"), and [Fontvieille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontvieille,_Monaco "Fontvieille, Monaco"). It is located at [43°43′51″N 7°25′26″E / 43.73083°N 7.42389°E](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Monaco-Ville&params=43_43_51_N_7_25_26_E_) and has an estimated population of 975. It has 19.64 hectares (48.5 acres) of surface area and is located between the districts of [Fontvieille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontvieille,_Monaco "Fontvieille, Monaco") and [La Condamine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Condamine "La Condamine").
Monaco-Ville was originally called **Monoikos** in [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"), after the temple of _Hercules Monoikos_, located in a [Phocaean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phocaea "Phocaea") colony of the 6th century BCE. During its history, Monoikos changed hands numerous times. It became _Monaco_ in the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"). Some of the [city walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_wall "City wall") and original structures still remain.

It was here that the Phocaeans of Massalia (now Marseille) founded the colony of Monoïkos in the 6th century BC. Monoikos was associated with Hercules, who was worshipped as Hercules Monoecus. According to the works of Hercules, but also according to Diodorus of Sicily and Strabo, the Greeks and the Ligurians reported that Hercules had passed through the region.
On 10 June 1215, a detachment of Ghibellines led by Fulco del Cassello began the construction of a fortress on the rock of Monaco in order to make it a strategic military position and a means of controlling the area.
They also established dwellings at the base of the Rock to support the garrisons. To attract the inhabitants of Genoa and the surrounding towns, they offered land and exempted newcomers from taxes.
On 8 January 1297, [François Grimaldi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Grimaldi "François Grimaldi"), descendant of Otto Canella, consul of Genoa in 1133, took over the fortress. Although he had a small army, he disguised himself as a Franciscan friar to enter, before opening the gates to his soldiers. This episode gave rise to his nickname, Malizia ("malice"). This is why today the arms of Monaco bear two Franciscans armed with a sword.
[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Monegasque_%E2%80%98Caruggi%E2%80%99.jpg/250px-Monegasque_%E2%80%98Caruggi%E2%80%99.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Monegasque_%E2%80%98Caruggi%E2%80%99.jpg)
View of the Old Town’s ‘caruggi’

Despite being located in the middle of the City of Monaco, the world's most densely populated urban center, Monaco-Ville remains a medieval village at heart, made up almost entirely of quiet pedestrian streets and marked by virtual silence after sundown. Though innumerable people visit Monaco-Ville and the palace square, only local vehicles are allowed up to the Rock, and gasoline-powered motorcycles are prohibited after 10 p.m.

It is famous for being the starting point of a torchlit religious procession by local residents that takes place on the eve of Good Friday each year.

texts.3:
#### **The Temple’s Story**
In 1952 the Charity Commissioner took over the temple’s affairs, and by court order a management trust was registered. The nine-member trust board is presently comprised of solicitors, chartered accountants, doctors and an industrialist. About 15,000 people visit daily, with the number going to over 25,000 on festival days.
Despite the cramped location and huge crowds, the temple is well maintained, clean and organized. As soon as one enters, it is impossible not to connect with the Goddess. Mumbadevi sits majestically on Her lion, infusing power and confidence in Her devotees as they surrender to Her. Adjoining the sanctum sanctorum of Mumbadevi is the imposing shrine of Jagadamba with Annapooraneshwari (both forms of the Goddess), showering benevolence on worshipers. The ornate walls with exquisite paintings of Gods and Goddesses blend into the divinely charged ambiance.
![Image 2](http://ds.hinduismtoday.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/f0037-01.jpg)
Some of the 15,000 visitors a day
The temple is open from 6:30am to 10 pm. As in all Devi temples, the celebration of Navaratri is of primacy. At Mumbadevi, four navaratris are celebrated in a year. Besides the Chaitra Navaratri (March/April) and Sharad Ashwin Navaratri (September/October), the lesser known Gupta Navaratris during Maagh (January/February) and Ashaada (June/July) are also celebrated.
The temple is one of the richest in the city. Its income is used to administer the temple and conduct festivities. “We are handling public money. We engage in charity and run an old age home in Ahmedabad. We provide scholarships to deserving students and medical aid to the poor. We also help other institutions engaged in social service,” confirms Jadhav.
texts.4:
#### **The Temple’s Story**
A few years back the temple ran into a controversy with reports of a government takeover. An investigation into the temple’s finances and administration by the Charity Commission found nothing amiss, and the issue was dropped. Following the infamous bomb blasts in 1993, three of which were in the vicinity of the temple, Mumbai police have greatly increased security in the area.
One devotee, Sushma Baadakar, told me of two great miracles in her life she attributes to the Goddess. The first, a property dispute, was resolved shortly after a chance visit to the temple in 2012 with her brother. She said, “The visit brought me under the protection of the Goddess.” Later, faced with cancer, she recounts, “At every stage of my treatment I saw miracles that left the doctors baffled. I still feel Mumbadevi is always with me, guiding every moment of my life.”
Whether Mumbai residents are aware of Mumbadevi or not, whether they visit her shrine or not, it is strongly believed that She protects anyone who comes to Her land. From the Ambanis to Bollywood stars and singers, innumerable people who came to this city seeking greener pastures, many of them with humble beginnings staying on pavements and railway platforms, have become rich and famous. Mumbadevi has remained true to Her legend as the wish-fulfilling Goddess who protects Her people.

texts.2: **Monaco-Ville** ([[mɔnakɔ vil]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French"); [Monégasque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mon%C3%A9gasque_dialect "Monégasque dialect"): _Mu̍negu-A̍utu_)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco-Ville#cite_note-1) is the southcentral [ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_divisions_of_Monaco "Administrative divisions of Monaco") in the [Principality of Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco-Ville#cite_note-2) Located on a [headland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headland "Headland") that extends into the [Mediterranean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco-Ville#cite_note-3) it is nicknamed [The Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_of_Monaco "Rock of Monaco") (French: _Le Rocher_; Monégasque: _A Roca_). It holds most of the country's political and judicial institutions: the [Prince's Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince's_Palace_of_Monaco "Prince's Palace of Monaco"), the [town hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipality_of_Monaco "Municipality of Monaco"), the government, the [National Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Council_(Monaco) "National Council (Monaco)") (parliament of Monaco), the [Municipal Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communal_Council_of_Monaco "Communal Council of Monaco"), the courts and a prison (hanging on The Rock).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco-Ville#cite_note-4)
texts.3:
Monaco-Ville is one of the four traditional [quarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarter_(urban_subdivision) "Quarter (urban subdivision)") ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _quartiers_) of Monaco; the others are [La Condamine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Condamine "La Condamine"), [Monte Carlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo "Monte Carlo"), and [Fontvieille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontvieille,_Monaco "Fontvieille, Monaco"). It is located at [43°43′51″N 7°25′26″E / 43.73083°N 7.42389°E](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Monaco-Ville&params=43_43_51_N_7_25_26_E_) and has an estimated population of 975. It has 19.64 hectares (48.5 acres) of surface area and is located between the districts of [Fontvieille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontvieille,_Monaco "Fontvieille, Monaco") and [La Condamine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Condamine "La Condamine").
Monaco-Ville was originally called **Monoikos** in [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"), after the temple of _Hercules Monoikos_, located in a [Phocaean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phocaea "Phocaea") colony of the 6th century BCE. During its history, Monoikos changed hands numerous times. It became _Monaco_ in the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"). Some of the [city walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_wall "City wall") and original structures still remain.
texts.4:
It was here that the Phocaeans of Massalia (now Marseille) founded the colony of Monoïkos in the 6th century BC. Monoikos was associated with Hercules, who was worshipped as Hercules Monoecus. According to the works of Hercules, but also according to Diodorus of Sicily and Strabo, the Greeks and the Ligurians reported that Hercules had passed through the region.
On 10 June 1215, a detachment of Ghibellines led by Fulco del Cassello began the construction of a fortress on the rock of Monaco in order to make it a strategic military position and a means of controlling the area.
They also established dwellings at the base of the Rock to support the garrisons. To attract the inhabitants of Genoa and the surrounding towns, they offered land and exempted newcomers from taxes.
On 8 January 1297, [François Grimaldi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Grimaldi "François Grimaldi"), descendant of Otto Canella, consul of Genoa in 1133, took over the fortress. Although he had a small army, he disguised himself as a Franciscan friar to enter, before opening the gates to his soldiers. This episode gave rise to his nickname, Malizia ("malice"). This is why today the arms of Monaco bear two Franciscans armed with a sword.

texts.5: Despite being located in the middle of the City of Monaco, the world's most densely populated urban center, Monaco-Ville remains a medieval village at heart, made up almost entirely of quiet pedestrian streets and marked by virtual silence after sundown. Though innumerable people visit Monaco-Ville and the palace square, only local vehicles are allowed up to the Rock, and gasoline-powered motorcycles are prohibited after 10 p.m.

**Raja Ravi Varma** (Malayalam:[[ɾaːd͡ʒaː ɾɐʋi ʋɐrmːɐ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Malayalam "Help:IPA/Malayalam")) (29 April 1848 – 2 October 1906[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-4)) was an Indian painter. His works are one of the best examples of the fusion of European [academic art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_art "Academic art") with a purely Indian sensibility and iconography. He greatly enhanced his reach and influence as a painter and public figure by making affordable [lithographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithography "Lithography") of his paintings available to the public. His lithographs increased the involvement of common people with fine arts and defined artistic tastes. His religious depictions of Hindu deities and works from [Indian epic poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_epic_poetry "Indian epic poetry") and [Puranas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puranas "Puranas") have received critical acclaim. He was part of the royal family of [Parappanad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parappanad "Parappanad"), [Malappuram district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malappuram_district "Malappuram district").
Raja Ravi Varma was closely related to the royal family of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") of present-day [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala") state in India. Later in his life, two of his granddaughters were adopted into the royal family.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-5)

Ry.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maha_Raja_Rajya_Shri "Maha Raja Rajya Shri") Ravi Varma ([Malayalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayalam_language "Malayalam language"): രവി വർമ്മ), [Koil Thampuran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koyi_Thampuran "Koyi Thampuran") of Kilimanoor at [Kilimanoor palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_palace "Kilimanoor palace") in the erstwhile [princely state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princely_state "Princely state") of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") (present-day [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"))[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-pal-6) into an aristocratic family that for over 200 years produced consorts for the princesses of the matrilineal Travancore royal family. The title [Raja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja "Raja") was conferred as a personal title by the Viceroy and Governor-General of India [Lord Curzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Curzon "Lord Curzon").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-pal-6)
[![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Raja_Ravi_Varma%2C_There_Comes_Papa_%281893%29.jpg/250px-Raja_Ravi_Varma%2C_There_Comes_Papa_%281893%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raja_Ravi_Varma,_There_Comes_Papa_(1893).jpg)

[_There comes Papa_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/There_Comes_Papa "There Comes Papa") (1893), depicting Varma's daughter Mahaprabha with one of her sons
[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Rani_Bharani_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi_of_Travancore_%281848%E2%80%931901%29.jpg/250px-Rani_Bharani_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi_of_Travancore_%281848%E2%80%931901%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rani_Bharani_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi_of_Travancore_(1848%E2%80%931901).jpg)
Varma's sister-in-law, [Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharani_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi "Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi"), Senior Rani of [Attingal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal "Attingal") (or [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Travancore "Kingdom of Travancore")), who adopted Varma's granddaughters in 1900

Ravi Varma was the son of Ezhumavil Neelakanthan Bhattatiripad and Uma Ambabayi Thampurratti. His mother Uma Ambabayi Thampuratty belonged to the baronial family which ruled the Kilimanoor [feudal estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") within the kingdom of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore"). She was a poet and writer, and her work _Parvati Swayamvaram_ was published by Varma after her death. Ravi Varma's father was a scholar of [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") and [Ayurveda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayurveda "Ayurveda") and hailed from the [Ernakulam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernakulam "Ernakulam") district in Kerala. Ravi Varma had two siblings, a sister named [Mangala Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangala_Bayi "Mangala Bayi") and a brother named [Raja Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Raja_Raja_Varma "C. Raja Raja Varma") (born 1860). The last-named was also a painter and worked closely with Ravi Varma all his life.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1866, at age 18, Varma was married to 12-year-old Bhageerthi Bayi (known formally as Pooruruttati Nal Bhageerathi Bayi Thampuratty) of the royal house of [Mavelikkara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mavelikkara "Mavelikkara"), another major [fief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") of Travancore kingdom. Notably, the house of Mavellikara was a branch of the Royal House of Travancore. Bhageerthi was the youngest of three sisters; her two elder siblings were adopted into the royal family of Travancore in 1857 to perpetuate the lineage. Designated the Senior and Junior Rani of Attingal, their descendants were vested with the succession to the throne of Travancore. Therefore, Ravi Varma's connection to the royal family became very close due to his marriage with Bhageerthi. His children would be royal by birth, since they belonged to their mother's family. The marriage, which was arranged by the parents in the proper Indian manner, was considered successful. The couple had five children, two sons, and three daughters. Their elder son, Kerala Varma (b.1876) was of an excessively spiritual temperament. He never married and eventually renounced the world, leaving home for good in 1912. The younger son, Rama Varma (born 1879), inherited his father's artistic talent and studied at the [JJ School of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JJ_School_of_Arts "JJ School of Arts"), [Mumbai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbai "Mumbai"). He was married to Gowri Kunjamma, sister of [Dewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewan "Dewan")[PGN Unnithan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGN_Unnithan "PGN Unnithan"), and became the father of seven children.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The three daughters of Ravi Varma and Bhageerthi Bayi were Mahaprabha Amma (who features in two of Varma's most famous paintings), Uma Amma (named after Varma's mother) and Cheria Kochamma. In 1900 CE, the Royal House of Travancore once again faced a succession crisis. Bhageerthi's two elder sisters, who had been adopted in order to carry forward the lineage, had failed to produce the desired heirs. They had six children between them, but only two of those survived, and both were boys (who also, incidentally, later died childless). According to the [matrilineal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrilineal "Matrilineal") Marumakkathayam system, the succession to the throne could only progress through females, and therefore it was necessary to make an adoption. Tradition dictated that two girls belonging to branches of the Royal Family be adopted together. They would be designated the Senior and Junior Rani of Attingal, and the succession to the throne of Travancore would be vested in their progeny, in accordance with the unusual and unique [Marumakkathayam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marumakkathayam "Marumakkathayam") system of succession.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Two of Varma's granddaughters were marked by destiny to receive this honour, the main reason being that they were the nearest matrilineal ([cognatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognatic "Cognatic")) kin to the incumbent Rani of Attingal. In August 1900, Mahaprabha's eldest daughter Lakshmi Bayi (aged 5 years) and Uma's eldest daughter Parvati Bayi (aged 4 years) were adopted into the Royal family of Travancore. It was [Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharani_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi "Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi"), their surviving grand-aunt, who formally adopted them. She died within one year of doing this, and the two girls were then installed as the Senior and Junior Ranis of [Attingal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal "Attingal") respectively. They were married while yet in their early teens to two gentlemen from suitable aristocratic families. It was the Junior Rani, [Sethu Parvathi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sethu_Parvathi_Bayi "Sethu Parvathi Bayi"), who gave birth to the much-awaited heir in 1912, exactly a day after her sixteenth birthday. Incidentally, her husband was a grand-nephew of Raja Ravi Varma and belonged to [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_Palace "Kilimanoor Palace"). The newborn child was the future Maharaja [Chithira Thirunal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chithira_Thirunal_Balarama_Varma "Chithira Thirunal Balarama Varma"), the last ruling [Maharaja of Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharaja_of_Travancore "Maharaja of Travancore").

He was followed by a brother (the future Maharaja [Marthanda Varma III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uthradom_Thirunal_Marthanda_Varma "Uthradom Thirunal Marthanda Varma")) and a sister [Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karthika_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi "Karthika Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi"), the mother of Maharaja [Rama Varma VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moolam_Thirunal_Rama_Varma "Moolam Thirunal Rama Varma") who is presently on the throne (since 2013). Meanwhile, the Senior Rani ([Sethu Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sethu_Lakshmi_Bayi "Sethu Lakshmi Bayi"), daughter of Mahaprabha Amma, and Regent from 1924 to 1931) also gave birth to two daughters later in life (in 1923 and 1926).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
In this way, the entire present (existing) royal family of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") is descended from Raja Ravi Varma. Well known among his royal descendants are the writers [Aswathi Thirunal Gowri Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswathi_Thirunal_Gowri_Lakshmi_Bayi "Aswathi Thirunal Gowri Lakshmi Bayi") and [Shreekumar Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shreekumar_Varma "Shreekumar Varma"), the artist [Rukmini Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rukmini_Varma "Rukmini Varma") and the classical musician [Aswathi Thirunal Rama Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswathi_Thirunal_Rama_Varma "Aswathi Thirunal Rama Varma").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Around Ravi Varma's 57th birthday he announced his decision to accept [Sanyasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanyasa "Sanyasa"), and retire from all worldly life when he turned 60. In his final years he suffered from grief for the death of Raja Raja Varma, and also from diabetes, which contributed to his death on 2 October 1906.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
Varma was patronised by [Ayilyam Thirunal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayilyam_Thirunal "Ayilyam Thirunal"), the next [Maharaja of Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharaja_of_Travancore "Maharaja of Travancore") and began formal training thereafter.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-The_Diary_of_C._Rajaraja_Varma-7) He learned the basics of painting in [Madurai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madurai "Madurai"). Later, he was trained in water painting by Rama Swami Naidu and rather reluctantly in [oil painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_painting "Oil painting") by British portraitist Theodore Jenson.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-8)
[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Raja_Ravi_Verma_Studio_Vadodara.jpg/250px-Raja_Ravi_Verma_Studio_Vadodara.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raja_Ravi_Verma_Studio_Vadodara.jpg)
The studio used by Varma during his stay at the [Laxmi Vilas Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laxmi_Vilas_Palace "Laxmi Vilas Palace")

The British administrator, [Edgar Thurston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Thurston "Edgar Thurston") was significant in promoting the careers of Varma and his brother.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-9) Varma received widespread acclaim after he won an award for an exhibition of his paintings at Vienna in 1873. Varma's paintings were also sent to the [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition") held in Chicago in 1893 and he was awarded three gold medals.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-10) He travelled throughout India in search of subjects. He often modelled Hindu [Goddesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goddess "Goddess") on [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_India "South India") women, whom he considered beautiful. Ravi Varma is particularly noted for his paintings depicting episodes from the story of [Dushyanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dushyanta "Dushyanta") and [Shakuntala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakuntala "Shakuntala"), and [Nala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nala "Nala") and [Damayanti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damayanti "Damayanti"), from the [Mahabharata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabharata "Mahabharata"). Ravi Varma's representation of [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu "Hindu") characters has become a part of the Indian imagination of the epics. He is often criticized for being too showy and sentimental in his style but his work remains very popular in India. Many of his fabulous paintings are housed at [Laxmi Vilas Palace, Vadodara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laxmi_Vilas_Palace,_Vadodara "Laxmi Vilas Palace, Vadodara").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-11)

## Raja Ravi Varma Press
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raja_Ravi_Varma&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Raja Ravi Varma Press")]
[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Raja_Ravi_Varma%2C_Mrs._Ramanadha_Rao.jpg/250px-Raja_Ravi_Varma%2C_Mrs._Ramanadha_Rao.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raja_Ravi_Varma,_Mrs._Ramanadha_Rao.jpg)
_Mrs. Ramanadha Rao and son_
Apparently on the advice of the then Dewan (Prime Minister) of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore"), [T. Madhava Rao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._Madhava_Rao "T. Madhava Rao"), Ravi Varma started a lithographic printing press in [Ghatkopar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghatkopar "Ghatkopar"), Mumbai in 1894 and later shifted it to Malavli near [Lonavala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonavala "Lonavala"), Maharashtra in 1899. The [oleographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleographs "Oleographs") produced by the press were mostly of Hindu gods and goddesses in scenes adapted mainly from the _[Mahabharata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabharata "Mahabharata")_, the _[Ramayana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramayana "Ramayana")_ and the _[Puranas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puranas "Puranas")_. These oleographs were very popular and continued to be printed in thousands for many years, even after the 1906 death of Ravi Varma.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Raja Ravi Varma Press
The Ravi Varma press was the largest and most innovative press in India at that time. The press was managed by Varma's brother, Raja Varma, but under their management, it was a commercial failure. By 1899 the press was deeply in debt and in 1901, the press was sold to his printing technician from Germany, Fritz Schleicher. Schleicher continued to print Ravi Varma's prints but later employed other artists to create new designs. Schleicher also broadened the product of press to include commercial and advertisement labels. Under the management of Schleicher and his successors, the press continued successfully until a devastating fire destroyed the whole factory in 1972. Many of Ravi Varma's original lithographic prints were also lost in the fire.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-12)

In 1904, [Viceroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroy_of_India "Viceroy of India")[Lord Curzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Curzon "Lord Curzon"), on behalf of the British King Emperor, bestowed upon Varma the [Kaisar-i-Hind Gold Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaisar-i-Hind_Gold_Medal "Kaisar-i-Hind Gold Medal"). A college dedicated to [fine arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_art "Fine art") was also constituted in his honour at [Mavelikara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mavelikara "Mavelikara"), [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"). Raja Ravi Varma High at [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor "Kilimanoor") was named after him and there are many cultural organizations throughout India bearing his name. In 2013, the crater Varma on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)") was named in his honor.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-13) Considering his vast contribution to [Indian art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_art "Indian art"), the Government of Kerala has instituted an award called [Raja Ravi Varma Puraskaram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma_Puraskaram "Raja Ravi Varma Puraskaram"), which is awarded every year to people who show excellence in the field of art and culture.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-14)
*   On his 65th death anniversary, India Post issued a commemorative postal stamp depicting Ravi Varma and his famous painting 'Damayanti and Swan'
Raja Ravi Varma is sometimes regarded as the first modern Indian artist due to his ability to reconcile Western aesthetics with Indian iconography. The Indian art historian and critic [Geeta Kapur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geeta_Kapur "Geeta Kapur") wrote,

## Raja Ravi Varma Press
> Ravi Varma is the indisputable father figure of modern Indian art. Naive and ambitious at the same time, he opens up the debate for his later compatriots in the specific matter of defining individual genius through professional acumen, of testing modes of cultural adaptation with idiosyncratic effect, of attempting pictorial narration with its historic scope.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-15)
Similarly, Baroda School artist [Gulam Mohammed Sheikh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulam_Mohammed_Sheikh "Gulam Mohammed Sheikh") also wrote about Ravi Varma as a modern artist. In his essay "Ravi Varma in Baroda", Sheikh asserted that Varma was a key figure in the establishment of Indian modern art, claiming that "the story of contemporary Indian art was never the same after Ravi Varma had entered it. He left his imprint on almost every aspect of it." Like Kapur, Sheikh praised Ravi Varma's integration of Indian and Western aesthetics and techniques, comparing him favorably to Indian modernist [Nandalal Bose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandalal_Bose "Nandalal Bose").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-16)

However, Ravi Varma's legacy is controversial. Fellow Baroda School artist and art historian [Ratan Parimoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratan_Parimoo "Ratan Parimoo") saw Ravi Varma in a less favorable light, derogatorily referring to him as [kitsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitsch "Kitsch") and claiming Varma's work was less spiritually authentic than folk art and tribal art. He argued that Ravi Varma was responsible for the "vulgarity" of popular art, comparing Varma's work to the lurid colors and sexuality of popular images in [calendar art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calendar_art?action=edit&redlink=1 "Calendar art (page does not exist)") and films.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-18) Australian art critic [Christopher Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Allen_(critic) "Christopher Allen (critic)") made the same points in his review of the 2026 exhibition _The God of Small Things: Faith and Popular Culture_ at the [Queensland Art Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland_Art_Gallery "Queensland Art Gallery").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-19)

**Ravi Varma** (born April 29, 1848, Kilimanoor Palace, near Trivandrum, Travancore [princely state](https://www.britannica.com/topic/princely-state-colonial-India), British India [now Thiruvananthapuram, [Kerala](https://www.britannica.com/place/Keralam), India]—died October 2, 1906, Kilimanoor Palace) was an Indian painter best known for uniting [Hindu](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hinduism) mythological subject matter with European realist and naturalist painting styles. He was one of the first Indian artists to use oil paints and to master the art of [lithographic](https://www.britannica.com/technology/lithography) reproduction of his work. In addition to incidents in Hindu mythology, Varma painted many portraits of Indian and British people in India.

## Early education in art
Varma was born into an aristocratic family in the [erstwhile](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/erstwhile) princely state of [Travancore](https://www.britannica.com/place/Travancore) in southwestern [India](https://www.britannica.com/place/India). He showed an interest in art from an early age, drawing on the walls of the family mansion with [chalk](https://www.britannica.com/art/chalk-drawing) and [charcoal](https://www.britannica.com/art/charcoal-drawing). His uncle Raja Raja Varma, an artist in his own right, noticed his passion for art and gave him his first [rudimentary](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/rudimentary) lessons in [painting](https://www.britannica.com/art/painting). When Varma was 13 or 14 years old, Ayilyam Thirunal, ruler of Travancore, became a patron of Varma’s early artistic career and allowed him to watch and learn from painters who practiced at the court. Varma was keen to learn [oil painting](https://www.britannica.com/art/oil-painting) but Ramaswamy Naidu, the only palace painter experienced in the medium at the time, refused to teach him, perhaps unwilling to give away his secrets to a potential rival. Arumugham Pillai, one of Naidu’s assistants, eventually taught Varma the basics of the technique in secret. Varma was later allowed to observe the oil painting of Theodore Jensen, a Danish-born British artist who came to the Travancore court in 1868, though Jensen also refused him formal training.

## Career as a professional artist


## Royal portraits
In 1870 Varma began his career as a professional painter—considered an inappropriate occupation for an [aristocrat](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/aristocrat) at the time—with a commissioned portrait of a family in Calicut (now [Kozhikode](https://www.britannica.com/place/Kozhikode)). Shortly afterward he painted a portrait of Thirunal and his wife, which led to his appointment as the palace artist at Trivandrum (now [Thiruvananthapuram](https://www.britannica.com/place/Thiruvananthapuram)). Varma won the Governor’s Gold Medal for the painting _Nair Lady Adorning Her Hair_ in 1873 and for _A Tamil Lady Playing the Sarabat_ the following year. These wins in India and another award at an [international exhibition](https://www.britannica.com/money/trade-show) in [Vienna](https://www.britannica.com/place/Vienna) made him a much-sought-after artist among both the Indian nobility and the Europeans in India, who commissioned him to paint their portraits.

Photo dated 2017.](https://cdn.britannica.com/13/229013-131-CF011E83/Tate-Modern-Switch-House-London-England.jpg) Britannica Quiz Can You Match These Lesser-Known Paintings to Their Artists?](https://www.britannica.com/quiz/can-you-match-these-lesser-known-paintings-to-their-artists)

## Mythology and religious themes
[Saraswati](https://cdn.britannica.com/42/74142-050-195AFA72/Hindu-deity-Sarasvati-painting-by-Rjaj-Ravi-Varma.jpg)This Ravi Varma painting depicts Saraswati, the Hindu goddess of learning and the arts, in white, holding a veena and a manuscript.
Alongside portraits, Varma increasingly painted subjects from Indian mythology. In 1876 his exhibition of _Shakuntala Writing a Love Letter to Dushyanta_, based on characters in the Indian epic [_Mahabharata_](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Mahabharata) and the subject of a [Sanskrit](https://www.britannica.com/art/Sanskrit-literature) play by poet [Kalidasa](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Kalidasa), was met with much acclaim. As his reputation grew, Varma was commissioned by royal families such as those of Baroda and Mysore to paint portraits and scenes from the _[Mahabharata](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Mahabharata)_ and another Indian epic, the _[Ramayana](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Ramayana-Indian-epic)_. His paintings, including _Harischandra in Distress_, _Jatayu Vadha_, and _Shri Rama Vanquishing the Sea_, captured dramatic moments from Indian mythology. He used European techniques of perspective and [composition](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/composition) to render realistic oil paintings of Hindu gods and goddesses as well as characters in the epics and the [Puranas](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Purana).

## Mythology and religious themes
Idealized depictions of women are [pervasive](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/pervasive) across Varma’s [oeuvre](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/oeuvre), both mythological and non-mythological. Often represented as sensuous and adorned in finely detailed [jewelry](https://www.britannica.com/art/jewelry) and [sari](https://www.britannica.com/topic/sari)s, these female forms are the predominant subjects of 10 paintings that Varma sent to the [World’s Columbian Exposition](https://www.britannica.com/event/Worlds-Columbian-Exposition) in [Chicago](https://www.britannica.com/place/Chicago) in 1893, where he was awarded two gold medals.
Did You Know?
In 1904 Varma was awarded the Kaiser-i-Hind, a medal to recognize distinguished public service in [British India](https://www.britannica.com/event/British-raj), which, until then, had been awarded exclusively to those engaged in trade and commerce. It was the inclusion of the title “Raja” in the [citation](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/citation) of this award that led to him being popularly called Raja Ravi Varma.

## Printing press
[Lakshmi](https://cdn.britannica.com/97/247597-050-87DC2FAB/Lakshmi-lithograph-Ravi-Varma-India-1894.jpg)The Hindu goddess Lakshmi, lithograph by Ravi Varma, c. 1894, one of a series of lithographs of Hindu gods by Varma.
In 1894 Varma set up a lithographic [press](https://www.britannica.com/technology/printing-press) in order to mass-produce copies of his paintings as [oleographs](https://www.britannica.com/technology/oleograph) (prints on cloth to resemble oil paintings), enabling ordinary people to afford them. Because of financial difficulties, he sold the press and the copyrights for many of his paintings seven years later to a German printing technician, who began printing Varma’s artwork on a wide variety of products, including [calendars](https://www.britannica.com/science/calendar) and matchboxes. Because the press enabled his artworks to be widely distributed, Varma’s images of Hindu gods and goddesses, especially those of [Saraswati](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Saraswati) and [Lakshmi](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Lakshmi), have become some of the most recognizable and enduring representations of these figures in Indian households.

## Legacy and criticism
Did You Know?
[Dadasaheb Phalke](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Dadasaheb-Phalke), considered the father of Indian [cinema](https://www.britannica.com/art/film), [collaborated](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/collaborated) closely with Ravi Varma’s press. He would go on to make India’s first feature film, _Raja Harishchandra_ (1913), and several other mythological films that borrowed heavily from Varma’s religious iconography.
Despite the dismissal of Varma’s work by some as “calendar art” because of its commercialization, interest in his work has remained constant. In 1997, for example, _The Begum’s Bath_ sold for a record price for an Indian artist at the time. Works such as _The Maharashtrian Lady_, _Shakuntala_, _The Milkmaid_, _Expectation_, and _Pleasing_ exhibit Varma’s characteristic sense of beauty and grace. Varma’s artworks and visual motifs have influenced cinema, [literature](https://www.britannica.com/art/literature), [advertisements](https://www.britannica.com/money/advertisement), [music](https://www.britannica.com/art/music), and popular [culture](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/culture), including a popular [comic book](https://www.britannica.com/art/comic-book) series on Indian mythology published by Amar Chitra Katha.

## Legacy and criticism
Varma was criticized severely by later artists who saw the content of his work as only superficially Indian because, despite depicting mythological Indian themes, it imitated Western styles of painting. That view was instrumental in the formation of the [Bengal School of Art](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Bengal-School-of-Art) (or Bengal school), whose members explored ancient Indian artistic traditions with a modernist sensibility. Varma’s representations of Indian women have sometimes been panned for being stereotypical, exclusionary, and overly eroticized.

**Raja Ravi Varma** (Malayalam:[[ɾaːd͡ʒaː ɾɐʋi ʋɐrmːɐ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Malayalam "Help:IPA/Malayalam")) (29 April 1848 – 2 October 1906[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-4)) was an Indian painter. His works are one of the best examples of the fusion of European [academic art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_art "Academic art") with a purely Indian sensibility and iconography. He greatly enhanced his reach and influence as a painter and public figure by making affordable [lithographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithography "Lithography") of his paintings available to the public. His lithographs increased the involvement of common people with fine arts and defined artistic tastes. His religious depictions of Hindu deities and works from [Indian epic poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_epic_poetry "Indian epic poetry") and [Puranas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puranas "Puranas") have received critical acclaim. He was part of the royal family of [Parappanad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parappanad "Parappanad"), [Malappuram district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malappuram_district "Malappuram district").
Raja Ravi Varma was closely related to the royal family of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") of present-day [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala") state in India. Later in his life, two of his granddaughters were adopted into the royal family.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-5)
texts.3:
Varma was born on 29 April 1848, as [M. R. Ry.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maha_Raja_Rajya_Shri "Maha Raja Rajya Shri") Ravi Varma ([Malayalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayalam_language "Malayalam language"): രവി വർമ്മ), [Koil Thampuran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koyi_Thampuran "Koyi Thampuran") of Kilimanoor at [Kilimanoor palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_palace "Kilimanoor palace") in the erstwhile [princely state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princely_state "Princely state") of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") (present-day [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"))[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-pal-6) into an aristocratic family that for over 200 years produced consorts for the princesses of the matrilineal Travancore royal family. The title [Raja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja "Raja") was conferred as a personal title by the Viceroy and Governor-General of India [Lord Curzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Curzon "Lord Curzon").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-pal-6)
[![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Raja_Ravi_Varma%2C_There_Comes_Papa_%281893%29.jpg/250px-Raja_Ravi_Varma%2C_There_Comes_Papa_%281893%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raja_Ravi_Varma,_There_Comes_Papa_(1893).jpg)
texts.4:
[_There comes Papa_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/There_Comes_Papa "There Comes Papa") (1893), depicting Varma's daughter Mahaprabha with one of her sons
[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Rani_Bharani_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi_of_Travancore_%281848%E2%80%931901%29.jpg/250px-Rani_Bharani_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi_of_Travancore_%281848%E2%80%931901%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rani_Bharani_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi_of_Travancore_(1848%E2%80%931901).jpg)
Varma's sister-in-law, [Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharani_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi "Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi"), Senior Rani of [Attingal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal "Attingal") (or [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Travancore "Kingdom of Travancore")), who adopted Varma's granddaughters in 1900
texts.5: Ravi Varma was the son of Ezhumavil Neelakanthan Bhattatiripad and Uma Ambabayi Thampurratti. His mother Uma Ambabayi Thampuratty belonged to the baronial family which ruled the Kilimanoor [feudal estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") within the kingdom of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore"). She was a poet and writer, and her work _Parvati Swayamvaram_ was published by Varma after her death. Ravi Varma's father was a scholar of [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") and [Ayurveda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayurveda "Ayurveda") and hailed from the [Ernakulam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernakulam "Ernakulam") district in Kerala. Ravi Varma had two siblings, a sister named [Mangala Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangala_Bayi "Mangala Bayi") and a brother named [Raja Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Raja_Raja_Varma "C. Raja Raja Varma") (born 1860). The last-named was also a painter and worked closely with Ravi Varma all his life.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
texts.6: In 1866, at age 18, Varma was married to 12-year-old Bhageerthi Bayi (known formally as Pooruruttati Nal Bhageerathi Bayi Thampuratty) of the royal house of [Mavelikkara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mavelikkara "Mavelikkara"), another major [fief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") of Travancore kingdom. Notably, the house of Mavellikara was a branch of the Royal House of Travancore. Bhageerthi was the youngest of three sisters; her two elder siblings were adopted into the royal family of Travancore in 1857 to perpetuate the lineage. Designated the Senior and Junior Rani of Attingal, their descendants were vested with the succession to the throne of Travancore. Therefore, Ravi Varma's connection to the royal family became very close due to his marriage with Bhageerthi. His children would be royal by birth, since they belonged to their mother's family. The marriage, which was arranged by the parents in the proper Indian manner, was considered successful. The couple had five children, two sons, and three daughters. Their elder son, Kerala Varma (b.1876) was of an excessively spiritual temperament. He never married and eventually renounced the world, leaving home for good in 1912. The younger son, Rama Varma (born 1879), inherited his father's artistic talent and studied at the [JJ School of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JJ_School_of_Arts "JJ School of Arts"), [Mumbai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbai "Mumbai"). He was married to Gowri Kunjamma, sister of [Dewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewan "Dewan")[PGN Unnithan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGN_Unnithan "PGN Unnithan"), and became the father of seven children.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
texts.7: The three daughters of Ravi Varma and Bhageerthi Bayi were Mahaprabha Amma (who features in two of Varma's most famous paintings), Uma Amma (named after Varma's mother) and Cheria Kochamma. In 1900 CE, the Royal House of Travancore once again faced a succession crisis. Bhageerthi's two elder sisters, who had been adopted in order to carry forward the lineage, had failed to produce the desired heirs. They had six children between them, but only two of those survived, and both were boys (who also, incidentally, later died childless). According to the [matrilineal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrilineal "Matrilineal") Marumakkathayam system, the succession to the throne could only progress through females, and therefore it was necessary to make an adoption. Tradition dictated that two girls belonging to branches of the Royal Family be adopted together. They would be designated the Senior and Junior Rani of Attingal, and the succession to the throne of Travancore would be vested in their progeny, in accordance with the unusual and unique [Marumakkathayam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marumakkathayam "Marumakkathayam") system of succession.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
texts.8: Two of Varma's granddaughters were marked by destiny to receive this honour, the main reason being that they were the nearest matrilineal ([cognatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognatic "Cognatic")) kin to the incumbent Rani of Attingal. In August 1900, Mahaprabha's eldest daughter Lakshmi Bayi (aged 5 years) and Uma's eldest daughter Parvati Bayi (aged 4 years) were adopted into the Royal family of Travancore. It was [Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharani_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi "Bharani Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi"), their surviving grand-aunt, who formally adopted them. She died within one year of doing this, and the two girls were then installed as the Senior and Junior Ranis of [Attingal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attingal "Attingal") respectively. They were married while yet in their early teens to two gentlemen from suitable aristocratic families. It was the Junior Rani, [Sethu Parvathi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sethu_Parvathi_Bayi "Sethu Parvathi Bayi"), who gave birth to the much-awaited heir in 1912, exactly a day after her sixteenth birthday. Incidentally, her husband was a grand-nephew of Raja Ravi Varma and belonged to [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_Palace "Kilimanoor Palace"). The newborn child was the future Maharaja [Chithira Thirunal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chithira_Thirunal_Balarama_Varma "Chithira Thirunal Balarama Varma"), the last ruling [Maharaja of Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharaja_of_Travancore "Maharaja of Travancore").
texts.9:
He was followed by a brother (the future Maharaja [Marthanda Varma III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uthradom_Thirunal_Marthanda_Varma "Uthradom Thirunal Marthanda Varma")) and a sister [Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karthika_Thirunal_Lakshmi_Bayi "Karthika Thirunal Lakshmi Bayi"), the mother of Maharaja [Rama Varma VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moolam_Thirunal_Rama_Varma "Moolam Thirunal Rama Varma") who is presently on the throne (since 2013). Meanwhile, the Senior Rani ([Sethu Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sethu_Lakshmi_Bayi "Sethu Lakshmi Bayi"), daughter of Mahaprabha Amma, and Regent from 1924 to 1931) also gave birth to two daughters later in life (in 1923 and 1926).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
In this way, the entire present (existing) royal family of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") is descended from Raja Ravi Varma. Well known among his royal descendants are the writers [Aswathi Thirunal Gowri Lakshmi Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswathi_Thirunal_Gowri_Lakshmi_Bayi "Aswathi Thirunal Gowri Lakshmi Bayi") and [Shreekumar Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shreekumar_Varma "Shreekumar Varma"), the artist [Rukmini Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rukmini_Varma "Rukmini Varma") and the classical musician [Aswathi Thirunal Rama Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aswathi_Thirunal_Rama_Varma "Aswathi Thirunal Rama Varma").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
texts.10:
Around Ravi Varma's 57th birthday he announced his decision to accept [Sanyasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanyasa "Sanyasa"), and retire from all worldly life when he turned 60. In his final years he suffered from grief for the death of Raja Raja Varma, and also from diabetes, which contributed to his death on 2 October 1906.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
Varma was patronised by [Ayilyam Thirunal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayilyam_Thirunal "Ayilyam Thirunal"), the next [Maharaja of Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharaja_of_Travancore "Maharaja of Travancore") and began formal training thereafter.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-The_Diary_of_C._Rajaraja_Varma-7) He learned the basics of painting in [Madurai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madurai "Madurai"). Later, he was trained in water painting by Rama Swami Naidu and rather reluctantly in [oil painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_painting "Oil painting") by British portraitist Theodore Jenson.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-8)
[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Raja_Ravi_Verma_Studio_Vadodara.jpg/250px-Raja_Ravi_Verma_Studio_Vadodara.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raja_Ravi_Verma_Studio_Vadodara.jpg)
The studio used by Varma during his stay at the [Laxmi Vilas Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laxmi_Vilas_Palace "Laxmi Vilas Palace")
texts.11: The British administrator, [Edgar Thurston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Thurston "Edgar Thurston") was significant in promoting the careers of Varma and his brother.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-9) Varma received widespread acclaim after he won an award for an exhibition of his paintings at Vienna in 1873. Varma's paintings were also sent to the [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World's_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition") held in Chicago in 1893 and he was awarded three gold medals.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-10) He travelled throughout India in search of subjects. He often modelled Hindu [Goddesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goddess "Goddess") on [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_India "South India") women, whom he considered beautiful. Ravi Varma is particularly noted for his paintings depicting episodes from the story of [Dushyanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dushyanta "Dushyanta") and [Shakuntala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakuntala "Shakuntala"), and [Nala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nala "Nala") and [Damayanti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damayanti "Damayanti"), from the [Mahabharata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabharata "Mahabharata"). Ravi Varma's representation of [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu "Hindu") characters has become a part of the Indian imagination of the epics. He is often criticized for being too showy and sentimental in his style but his work remains very popular in India. Many of his fabulous paintings are housed at [Laxmi Vilas Palace, Vadodara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laxmi_Vilas_Palace,_Vadodara "Laxmi Vilas Palace, Vadodara").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-11)

## Raja Ravi Varma Press
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Raja_Ravi_Varma&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Raja Ravi Varma Press")]
[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Raja_Ravi_Varma%2C_Mrs._Ramanadha_Rao.jpg/250px-Raja_Ravi_Varma%2C_Mrs._Ramanadha_Rao.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raja_Ravi_Varma,_Mrs._Ramanadha_Rao.jpg)
_Mrs. Ramanadha Rao and son_
Apparently on the advice of the then Dewan (Prime Minister) of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore"), [T. Madhava Rao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._Madhava_Rao "T. Madhava Rao"), Ravi Varma started a lithographic printing press in [Ghatkopar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghatkopar "Ghatkopar"), Mumbai in 1894 and later shifted it to Malavli near [Lonavala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonavala "Lonavala"), Maharashtra in 1899. The [oleographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleographs "Oleographs") produced by the press were mostly of Hindu gods and goddesses in scenes adapted mainly from the _[Mahabharata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabharata "Mahabharata")_, the _[Ramayana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramayana "Ramayana")_ and the _[Puranas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puranas "Puranas")_. These oleographs were very popular and continued to be printed in thousands for many years, even after the 1906 death of Ravi Varma.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
texts.13:
## Raja Ravi Varma Press
The Ravi Varma press was the largest and most innovative press in India at that time. The press was managed by Varma's brother, Raja Varma, but under their management, it was a commercial failure. By 1899 the press was deeply in debt and in 1901, the press was sold to his printing technician from Germany, Fritz Schleicher. Schleicher continued to print Ravi Varma's prints but later employed other artists to create new designs. Schleicher also broadened the product of press to include commercial and advertisement labels. Under the management of Schleicher and his successors, the press continued successfully until a devastating fire destroyed the whole factory in 1972. Many of Ravi Varma's original lithographic prints were also lost in the fire.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-12)

## Raja Ravi Varma Press
In 1904, [Viceroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroy_of_India "Viceroy of India")[Lord Curzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Curzon "Lord Curzon"), on behalf of the British King Emperor, bestowed upon Varma the [Kaisar-i-Hind Gold Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaisar-i-Hind_Gold_Medal "Kaisar-i-Hind Gold Medal"). A college dedicated to [fine arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_art "Fine art") was also constituted in his honour at [Mavelikara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mavelikara "Mavelikara"), [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"). Raja Ravi Varma High at [Kilimanoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor "Kilimanoor") was named after him and there are many cultural organizations throughout India bearing his name. In 2013, the crater Varma on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)") was named in his honor.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-13) Considering his vast contribution to [Indian art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_art "Indian art"), the Government of Kerala has instituted an award called [Raja Ravi Varma Puraskaram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma_Puraskaram "Raja Ravi Varma Puraskaram"), which is awarded every year to people who show excellence in the field of art and culture.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-14)

Raja Ravi Varma is sometimes regarded as the first modern Indian artist due to his ability to reconcile Western aesthetics with Indian iconography. The Indian art historian and critic [Geeta Kapur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geeta_Kapur "Geeta Kapur") wrote,

## Raja Ravi Varma Press
> Ravi Varma is the indisputable father figure of modern Indian art. Naive and ambitious at the same time, he opens up the debate for his later compatriots in the specific matter of defining individual genius through professional acumen, of testing modes of cultural adaptation with idiosyncratic effect, of attempting pictorial narration with its historic scope.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-15)
Similarly, Baroda School artist [Gulam Mohammed Sheikh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulam_Mohammed_Sheikh "Gulam Mohammed Sheikh") also wrote about Ravi Varma as a modern artist. In his essay "Ravi Varma in Baroda", Sheikh asserted that Varma was a key figure in the establishment of Indian modern art, claiming that "the story of contemporary Indian art was never the same after Ravi Varma had entered it. He left his imprint on almost every aspect of it." Like Kapur, Sheikh praised Ravi Varma's integration of Indian and Western aesthetics and techniques, comparing him favorably to Indian modernist [Nandalal Bose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandalal_Bose "Nandalal Bose").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-16)

However, Ravi Varma's legacy is controversial. Fellow Baroda School artist and art historian [Ratan Parimoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratan_Parimoo "Ratan Parimoo") saw Ravi Varma in a less favorable light, derogatorily referring to him as [kitsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitsch "Kitsch") and claiming Varma's work was less spiritually authentic than folk art and tribal art. He argued that Ravi Varma was responsible for the "vulgarity" of popular art, comparing Varma's work to the lurid colors and sexuality of popular images in [calendar art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calendar_art?action=edit&redlink=1 "Calendar art (page does not exist)") and films.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-18) Australian art critic [Christopher Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Allen_(critic) "Christopher Allen (critic)") made the same points in his review of the 2026 exhibition _The God of Small Things: Faith and Popular Culture_ at the [Queensland Art Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland_Art_Gallery "Queensland Art Gallery").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-19)

**Ravi Varma** (born April 29, 1848, Kilimanoor Palace, near Trivandrum, Travancore [princely state](https://www.britannica.com/topic/princely-state-colonial-India), British India [now Thiruvananthapuram, [Kerala](https://www.britannica.com/place/Keralam), India]—died October 2, 1906, Kilimanoor Palace) was an Indian painter best known for uniting [Hindu](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Hinduism) mythological subject matter with European realist and naturalist painting styles. He was one of the first Indian artists to use oil paints and to master the art of [lithographic](https://www.britannica.com/technology/lithography) reproduction of his work. In addition to incidents in Hindu mythology, Varma painted many portraits of Indian and British people in India.
texts.1:
## Early education in art
Varma was born into an aristocratic family in the [erstwhile](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/erstwhile) princely state of [Travancore](https://www.britannica.com/place/Travancore) in southwestern [India](https://www.britannica.com/place/India). He showed an interest in art from an early age, drawing on the walls of the family mansion with [chalk](https://www.britannica.com/art/chalk-drawing) and [charcoal](https://www.britannica.com/art/charcoal-drawing). His uncle Raja Raja Varma, an artist in his own right, noticed his passion for art and gave him his first [rudimentary](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/rudimentary) lessons in [painting](https://www.britannica.com/art/painting). When Varma was 13 or 14 years old, Ayilyam Thirunal, ruler of Travancore, became a patron of Varma’s early artistic career and allowed him to watch and learn from painters who practiced at the court. Varma was keen to learn [oil painting](https://www.britannica.com/art/oil-painting) but Ramaswamy Naidu, the only palace painter experienced in the medium at the time, refused to teach him, perhaps unwilling to give away his secrets to a potential rival. Arumugham Pillai, one of Naidu’s assistants, eventually taught Varma the basics of the technique in secret. Varma was later allowed to observe the oil painting of Theodore Jensen, a Danish-born British artist who came to the Travancore court in 1868, though Jensen also refused him formal training.
texts.3:
## Royal portraits
In 1870 Varma began his career as a professional painter—considered an inappropriate occupation for an [aristocrat](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/aristocrat) at the time—with a commissioned portrait of a family in Calicut (now [Kozhikode](https://www.britannica.com/place/Kozhikode)). Shortly afterward he painted a portrait of Thirunal and his wife, which led to his appointment as the palace artist at Trivandrum (now [Thiruvananthapuram](https://www.britannica.com/place/Thiruvananthapuram)). Varma won the Governor’s Gold Medal for the painting _Nair Lady Adorning Her Hair_ in 1873 and for _A Tamil Lady Playing the Sarabat_ the following year. These wins in India and another award at an [international exhibition](https://www.britannica.com/money/trade-show) in [Vienna](https://www.britannica.com/place/Vienna) made him a much-sought-after artist among both the Indian nobility and the Europeans in India, who commissioned him to paint their portraits.
[![Image 1: Tate Modern extension Switch House, London, England. (Tavatnik, museums). Photo dated 2017.](https://cdn.britannica.com/13/229013-131-CF011E83/Tate-Modern-Switch-House-London-England.jpg) Britannica Quiz Can You Match These Lesser-Known Paintings to Their Artists?](https://www.britannica.com/quiz/can-you-match-these-lesser-known-paintings-to-their-artists)
